strengths: The paper introduces a well-designed, two-stage pretraining framework (SPECTRE) that effectively combines local self-supervised representation learning (DINOv3-based) with global vision-language alignment (SigLIP-based), addressing the specific challenges of volumetric CT imaging.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across diverse tasks: 3D tumor biomarker classification (6 datasets), semantic segmentation (4 datasets), and zero-shot cross-modal retrieval (2 datasets), comparing against a large number (11) of existing state-of-the-art CT foundation models.
Outstanding commitment to open science and reproducibility by training exclusively on publicly available datasets and promising to fully open-source the model, pretraining recipes, and training code.

Strong empirical performance, achieving state-of-the-art results in biomarker classification and demonstrating highly competitive segmentation capability using a simplified encoder-only masked transformer setup (SEoMT).
weaknesses: Most core architectural and loss components (such as DINOv3, SigLIP, 3D RoPE, and the Encoder-only Mask Transformer) are adapted from existing 2D and 3D literature, representing a solid engineering integration rather than fundamentally new theoretical or architectural breakthroughs.

The computational resources required for pretraining (24 Blackwell B200 GPUs) are exceptionally high, which may hinder direct reproducibility or adaptation of the pretraining pipeline by resource-constrained academic labs, although the release of model weights significantly alleviates this.

The simplified, decoder-free segmentation head (SEoMT) occasionally struggles with fine-grained boundaries or very small lesions compared to highly-optimized convolutional decoders like nnU-Net, indicating a potential trade-off between architectural simplicity and dense prediction precision.

strengths: Highly scalable and clinically well-grounded two-stage pretraining framework (SPECTRE) that effectively combines self-supervised learning (DINOv3 style) with vision-language alignment (SigLIP) for volumetric CT.

Presents an elegant dual-transformer architecture (local ViTl and global ViTg) to address the quadratic computational complexity of 3D self-attention, preserving both local geometric detail and global context.
Strictly utilizes open, publicly available datasets for pretraining, promoting transparency and reproducibility in medical foundation model research.
Extensive and rigorous downstream evaluation spanning frozen-embedding biomarker classification, zero-shot cross-modal retrieval, and dense semantic segmentation on multiple clinical benchmarks.
weaknesses: The core architectural components (such as 3D RoPE, DINOv3, and SigLIP) are largely existing blocks adapted for this domain, meaning the novelty is primarily in successful engineering, scaling, and execution rather than fundamental theoretical breakthroughs.

The decoder-free SEoMT segmentation method predicts masks at 1/4 resolution and relies on trilinear interpolation, which struggles to capture fine boundary details for very small or low-contrast lesions.
The pretraining dataset is heavily skewed towards thoracic imaging (e.g., NLST, CT-RATE), leading to slightly less pronounced performance gains in some abdominal tasks.

strengths: A well-designed, scalable hierarchical transformer architecture (local window ViT + global scan ViT) that elegantly handles the memory and computational constraints of volumetric 3D CT data.
A rigorous two-stage pretraining recipe combining dense local self-supervised learning (DINOv3/iBOT) with global cross-modal semantic alignment (SigLIP).

Comprehensive and standardized evaluation across multiple diverse benchmarks: 6 biomarker classification datasets (using frozen kNN), 4 semantic segmentation datasets (via an encoder-only mask transformer), and 2 text-image retrieval datasets.
Strong commitment to reproducibility and open science, training exclusively on openly available CT datasets (229k scans) and promising public release of all code, training recipes, and weights.
Excellent presentation, clear writing, and informative visualizations (e.g., architecture overview, saliency maps, and UMAP embeddings).
weaknesses: The individual methodology components (DINOv3, SigLIP, 3D RoPE, EoMT) are largely adapted from existing computer vision and medical imaging literature, making the primary contribution more of a solid engineering/scaling recipe rather than fundamental algorithmic novelty.

For semantic segmentation (Table 1), while SPECTRE outperforms prior transformer-based models, it still slightly underperforms the optimized CNN-based nnU-Net baseline on some datasets (e.g., AMOS-CT), likely due to the 1/4 resolution prediction and simple trilinear interpolation which can smooth out fine details.

In Table 3, the Merlin model still outperforms SPECTRE on the Findings-to-image retrieval task by a large margin (77.6% vs 55.5% Recall@1). The authors should further dissect why this gap exists despite SPECTRE's larger scale and two-stage pretraining.

strengths: The paper addresses the practical challenges of training large-scale 3D Vision Transformers for CT (e.g., cubic scaling of tokens, geometric anisotropy) with a well-motivated local-to-global hierarchical transformer architecture.

A rigorous, multi-faceted evaluation is conducted across 11 state-of-the-art CT foundation models, spanning biomarker classification (using frozen kNN), semantic segmentation, and zero-shot cross-modal retrieval.

The pretraining is performed entirely on publicly available datasets (comprising nearly 230k scans), and the authors commit to making the code, pretraining recipes, and model weights fully open-source, which is highly valuable for the medical imaging community.

The proposed two-stage pretraining framework (local SSL with DINOv3 + global VLA with SigLIP) is technically sound, incorporating modern techniques like 3D Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), RoPE-box jittering, and LLM-paraphrased reports to ensure robustness.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic components (e.g., DINOv3, SigLIP, RoFormer/RoPE, LoRA) are mostly adapted from existing natural image and NLP domains rather than being fundamentally novel machine learning designs.

The pretraining dataset is heavily skewed towards chest/thoracic scans (e.g., NLST, CT-RATE, and INSPECT comprise approximately 203k out of the 229k total scans), which may limit representation quality in less-represented anatomical regions, though the downstream abdominal evaluations still show strong transfer.

The lightweight encoder-only segmentation evaluation (SEoMT) struggles on very small structures (<10mm) due to the 1/4 resolution feature grid and trilinear upsampling, although the authors successfully demonstrate that using a stronger decoder (e.g., UNETR) mitigates this limitation.

strengths: Pragmatic and well-designed architecture: The local-to-global ($ViT_\ell$ and $ViT_g$) dual-stage transformer efficiently scales to high-resolution 3D volumetric data, overcoming the cubic complexity of 3D tokenization while maintaining local patch geometries and global context.

Well-structured pretraining pipeline: The two-stage training (SSL via DINOv3 followed by VLA via SigLIP) successfully combines high-resolution structural priors with semantic clinical language features.

Extensive and rigorous benchmarking: The paper evaluates SPECTRE against 11 prior state-of-the-art CT foundation models across multiple tasks (biomarker classification, semantic segmentation, and zero-shot cross-modal retrieval), demonstrating superior or highly competitive performance.

Commitment to open science: Training exclusively on publicly accessible datasets and releasing all code, pretraining recipes, and weights ensures high reproducibility and lowers the entry barrier for medical AI researchers.
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: The individual components of the pipeline (DINOv3, SigLIP, 3D RoPE, and Qwen with LoRA) are largely adaptations of existing models and loss functions rather than entirely new foundational concepts.

Slightly lower performance in some dense segmentation tasks: While the proposed SEoMT is elegant and uses an encoder-only configuration, it is occasionally outperformed by dedicated decoder-heavy models (e.g., CT-FM) on complex anatomy segmentation tasks.

Anatomical pretraining bias: As noted by the authors, the pretraining datasets are heavily skewed towards thoracic imaging (e.g., NLST, CT-RATE, and INSPECT), which may limit optimal generalization on pelvic or musculoskeletal CT tasks.

strengths: Substantial curation of open data: The paper pretrains on a massive cohort of 229,619 publicly available 3D CT scans, proving that high-performing 3D medical foundation models can be built entirely without relying on closed/private datasets.

Commitment to open-source: The authors commit to releasing the model weights, pretraining recipes, and training code, which is a highly valuable resource for the 3D medical imaging research community.

Diverse and comprehensive evaluation: The proposed model is benchmarked across three distinct axes: cancer biomarker classification (6 datasets), 3D semantic segmentation (6 datasets in total), and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval (2 datasets).

Solid system design: The combination of a local window-based 3D transformer (ViT_l) and a global aggregator (ViT_g) successfully addresses the quadratic token explosion issue in high-resolution volumetric CT scans.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The work primarily integrates and scales up existing concepts (such as DINOv3, SigLIP, 3D RoPE, and Qwen3 text embeddings with LoRA) rather than introducing novel architectural paradigms or pretraining losses.

Underwhelming segmentation performance: Despite the massive pretraining on ~230k volumes, SPECTRE underperforms conventional supervised non-foundation models like nnU-Net ResEnc L (Table 1) and other CT foundation models like CT-FM (Table 9) in semantic segmentation.

Inconsistent zero-shot retrieval results: In the text-to-image retrieval benchmarks (Table 3), SPECTRE is significantly outperformed by the Merlin model on 'Findings' retrieval (e.g., 55.5% vs. 77.6% Recall@1 for N=32), casting doubt on the absolute superiority of the vision-language alignment.

Absence of critical pretraining ablations: The paper lacks a rigorous ablation study demonstrating the isolated impact of the two pretraining stages. It is important to show how the model performs with Stage 1 (SSL-only) vs. Stage 2 (VLA-only) across all downstream tasks to justify the dual-stage complexity.

Extreme computational barrier: Pretraining requires massive industrial resources (24 Blackwell B200 GPUs with 4.32 TB of GPU memory), which makes academic replication, verification, and customization extremely difficult.
